- When sentiment is consistently positive (≥0.6) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast by 1–3% for next period.
- When sentiment is negative (≤0.2) or volatile, model often underestimates; increase forecast by 1–3% to compensate for downward bias.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., +5%+ in 3–5 days), model frequently overshoots in subsequent days; apply a 2–5 day decay filter to smooth out overreaction.
- If sentiment shifts from negative to positive mid-horizon, model often fails to adjust; check for sudden reversal and adjust forecast mid-series by +1–2%.
- Mean reversion is strong in 3–5 day horizons; if forecast is >10% above recent 7-day average, reduce by 1–2% per day until convergence.
- For 30-day forecasts, model often ignores sentiment momentum; if sentiment is trending upward, add 0.5–1.5% to forecast for next 5–7 days.
- If sentiment is low (≤0.2) and price is falling, model underestimates further drops; add 0.5–1.5% buffer to forecast to avoid under-shock.
- Avoid overfitting to recent highs; if last 3–5 days are above 65, cap forecast at 65–68 unless sentiment strongly bullish.
- If sentiment is neutral (0.2–0.6) and price is trending, model often misjudges direction; use sentiment-weighted average of 3–5 day mean to anchor forecast.
